title: Vātaṃ prāṇam: holding on to Prajāpati
theme: Prajāpati, who is the wind outside and the breath within and guards the world, is held on to in thought and asked to keep the speakers from death and harm until old age.

words.context: The anonymous commentator: «वातमन्तरिक्षस्थवायुरूपम्» — in the form of the wind that moves in the mid-air
The anonymous commentator: «प्राणं समस्तपिण्डाण्डस्थप्राणापानादिरूपम्» — in the form of the in-breath, out-breath and the rest in every body
The anonymous commentator: «मनसाऽन्तरङ्गेणान्वारभामहे» — with the mind, the inner faculty

words.meaning: we lay hold of, hold on to

words.context: The anonymous commentator: «तं प्रजापतिं परमात्मानं» — that Prajāpati, the supreme self
The anonymous commentator: «भुवनस्य ब्रह्माण्डस्य गोपा रक्षकः» — the protector of the world-egg, the universe

words.role: first verb of the second line

words.context: The anonymous commentator: «अंहसः पापाच्च पातु» — guard us from sin too
The anonymous commentator: «ज्योग्जीवाश्विरंजीवनाः सन्तो वयं» — we, living long
The anonymous commentator: «वार्धकावस्थामशीमहि प्राप्नुमः» — may we reach the state of old age

sandhi.rule: manasā + anvārabhāmahe → manasānvārabhāmahe; the avagraha marks the merged a (P. 6.1.101 (अकः सवर्णे दीर्घः)).

sandhi.type: saḥ before a consonant; visarga before t
sandhi.rule: saḥ loses its visarga before a consonant (P. 6.1.132 (एतत्तदोः सुलोपोऽकोरनञ्समासे हलि)); naḥ → no before m (P. 6.1.114 (हशि च)); mṛtyoḥ + trāyatām → mṛtyos trāyatām (P. 8.3.34 (विसर्जनीयस्य सः)).

sandhi.type: k before a voiced consonant; -āḥ before a voiced consonant
sandhi.rule: jyok → jyog before j (P. 8.2.39 (झलां जशोऽन्ते)); jīvāḥ drops its visarga before j; jarām + aśīmahi joins without change.

morphology.note: An optative of the root aorist of √aś ‘to reach’ (aś-ī-mahi), middle; the commentator renders it with a present, prāpnumaḥ.
A root noun in -ā (gopā, ‘cow-protector’, then any guardian); the nominative singular is gopāḥ.

translation.literal: The wind, the breath, we lay hold of with the mind: Prajāpati, who is the guardian of the world. May he protect us from death, may he guard us from distress; living long, may we reach old age.
translation.readable: With our minds we hold on to Prajāpati, the wind and the breath, the guardian of the world. May he keep us from death and from harm, so that we live long and reach old age.

anvaya: यः भुवनस्य गोपाः [तम्] वातम् प्राणम् प्रजापतिम् मनसा अन्वारभामहे । सः नः मृत्योः त्रायताम् अंहसः पातु । ज्योक् जीवाः जराम् अशीमहि ।
syntax: A main clause in the first person plural (anvārabhāmahe) with Prajāpati as object, described by two appositives (vātam, prāṇam) and a relative clause; then two imperatives with saḥ as subject, and an optative wish of the speakers.

ambiguities.note: The commentator reads the two words as one being in two forms: the breath in every body and the wind in the mid-air, so that Prajāpati sustains both the body and the universe («एतेन पिण्डाण्डब्रह्माण्डोभयविधारकत्वं प्रजापतेरुक्तं भवति»).

metre.name: triṣṭubh
metre.note: A triṣṭubh verse with irregular pādas; the checker counts 23 and 20 syllables. The first pāda (vātaṃ prāṇaṃ manasānvārabhāmahe) has 12, and the last (jyog jīvā jarām aśīmahi) only 8.

beginner: This verse asks for a long life. It names Prajāpati, the lord of creatures, and says that he is both the wind that blows through the sky and the breath that moves in each body. The old commentator explains that this shows Prajāpati holding up both the single body and the whole universe. The speakers say that they hold on to him with their minds, the way one might take hold of a support. Then they ask him to protect them from death and from harm. The last words are a wish many people share: that we may live long and grow old. The commentator explains that this means living out a full human span of life.
analogy: Like keeping a hand on a railing in the dark: the support is the same one that holds up the whole stair.

commentary.label: direct
commentary.text: That Prajāpati, held on to in the mind, protect the speakers from death and distress, so that they live long and reach old age.

commentary.label: traditional
commentary.text: The anonymous commentator: the supreme self, the breath in every body and the wind of the mid-air, the protector of the universe: «तं प्रजापतिं परमात्मानं».

commentary.q: What does reaching old age mean?
commentary.label: traditional
commentary.text: The anonymous commentator: living long, may we reach the state of old age, that is, live a full human span («ज्योग्जीवाश्विरंजीवनाः सन्तो वयं», «वार्धकावस्थामशीमहि प्राप्नुमः»).

schools.disagreement: No Vedānta-school commentary on this verse is in the edition’s sources. Only the anonymous commentator comments on it, and his reading is a prayer to the Lord (paramātman) without a school argument; Sāyaṇa’s and Bhāskara’s files contain no comment on this verse, and Raṅgarāmānuja’s commentary on the Mahānārāyaṇa is not among the sources.

contemporary.text: The verse’s last wish is not for glory but to grow old. Wanting a full, ordinary span of life is one of the oldest hopes people have put into words. This is a modern reflection on the passage, not part of its traditional meaning.

reflect.beginner: What would you hope to be doing when you are old?
reflect.deeper: Why might the same being be named as both the wind and the breath?
reflect.practice: Sit for a minute and notice your breath going in and out, without changing it.

references.text: Only the anonymous commentator comments on this anuvāka; the edition’s Sāyaṇa and Bhāskara files have no comment on it (the concordance maps are empty here, correctly).

The footnote printed at the end of this anuvāka in the edition’s anonymous-commentary file (Sāyaṇa on TA 6.7) belongs to the previous verse, paraṃ mṛtyo (10.46); it is the Ānandāśrama editor’s, not the commentator’s.
